nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
April 19, 1990.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

Common Name: Blue crab
Scientific Name: Callinectes sapidus

FLELMR CODE: 5660

Other Common Names: Jimmies (males), sooks (adult females); common edible crab.

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
	Family: Portunidae

Note: 	Subphylum: Crustacea

nodes.title: Range
nodes.body:
Overall: Blue crab is a cosmopolitan species found in coastal waters, primarily in bays and brackish estuaries. The original range was from Nova Scotia and Maine to northern Argentina (767) .

Within the Study Area: It is abundant throughout the near shore and estuarine areas in
the Gulf of Mexico.

Migration and Movements
Migrations within estuarine systems are related to phases of life cycle, season, and to a lesser extent search for favorable environmental conditions. Most crabs move to relatively deeper, warmer waters during winter and return to rivers, tidal creeks, salt marshes and sounds when conditions become more favorable. Megalopae are recruited into estuarine waters followed by migration of early juvenile stages of both sexes upstream to lower salinity waters (686). In the Gulf of Mexico, immature females approaching their final molt during the spring, migrate to lower salinities to mate, then these females migrate back to higher salinity waters during June and July (3). Adult males appear to remain in lower salinity waters and rarely move to high salinity. Adult crabs rarely migrate between estuaries (3).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: The eggs are carried by the female; when bearing the eggs the female is commonly referred to as a sponge crab. These females are found in 23-33 ppt and 19-29 C waters. Zoeae are planktonic and estuarine to oceanic. The megalopae swim freely and may be found in the surf area near the bottom in near shore or lower estuarine high-salinity areas. Juveniles and adults tend to be demersal and estuarine. Adult males spend most of their time in low salinity waters; females move into these lower salinities as they approach their terminal molt to mate. After mating, females move to higher salinity areas of estuaries and near shore environments for spawning.

nodes.title: Habitat
nodes.body:
Type: Depending on life stage, blue crabs are neritic, estuarine and riverine. Zoea are positively phototrophic (147).

Substrate: Juveniles and adults are found on muddy and sandy shores of the east and gulf coasts.

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Tolerance limits for adults and juveniles range from 3-37 C, but are highly dependent on acclimation and salinity (705). The interaction of salinity and temperature reveals blue crabs to be less tolerant of low salinities at high temperatures and high salinities at low temperatures (455). The species has been found from 3-33 C. Adults cease feeding at temperatures around 10 C and burrow in mud at 5 C. Adult males are more tolerant of temperature extremes than females.

Salinity: Tolerant of extremes, the species has been found from freshwater to hypersaline lagoons (0-50 ppt). Early zoeae are found at high salinities, usually 20 ppt or greater (182). Megalopae may be transported to somewhat lower salinities. Juvenile, ?first crab?, gradually move into less saline waters (2-21 ppt most desirable). Reported values for juveniles vary and specific salinity levels are not critical to post larval crabs. Adult males are usually found at less than 10 ppt. Blue crabs are less tolerant of low salinities and high temperatures or of high salinities and low temperatures.

Dissolved Oxygen: Low dissolved oxygen concentrations coupled with high temperatures often results in high local mortalities throughout the summer season.

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Repro Mode: Sexual, dioecious, internal fertilization.

Mating and Spawning: Mating normally occurs in low salinity waters in the upper reaches of tidal creeks and rivers at the females terminal molt. Females may ovulate more than once and sperm can survive for at least one year in the female`s seminal receptacle. Eggs are fertilized as they are passed from the ovaries to the seminal receptacle and are extruded out to the pleopods (473).

Season: In the Gulf of Mexico, two peak spawning periods typically occur, early spring and early fall (355 492).

Reproductive Capacity: 1.75 to 2 million eggs are produced per spawn.

nodes.title: Growth
nodes.body:
Egg: When first extruded eggs are about 0.25 mrn. Hatching occurs at 14-17 days at 26 C and 12-14 days at 29 C; hatching does not appear to occur at salinities below 15 ppt (146 166).

Larva: Larvae 0.25 mm at hatching develop through 7 zoeal stages (approximately 31-49 days at 25 C and 26 ppt), the final zoeal stage is about 1.0 mrn in width. The last zoeal stage metamorphoses into a megalopa lasting 6-12 days, at optimum salinity (30 ppt) and temperature (25 C), before molting to the ?first crab? stage or juvenile at 2.2-3.0 mm (145).

Juvenile: Growth and maturation occur through a series of molts. Growth and molting stop during winter.

Adults: Blue crabs mature in approximately 10-12 months on the Gulf coast, while temperate populations may take up to 20 months (473). Females have varied in size from mature at 51 mm to immature at 177 mm. Females mate at their terminal molt, males continue to grow and molt after reaching sexual maturity. Blue crabs have an estimated life span of 3-4 years (704). Males are typically heavier than females of the same size. Growth equations for crabs > 25 mm CW are log W= -3.74 + 2.77 log (CW) male and log W= 3.54 + 2.64 log (CW) (575).

Food and Feeding
Blue crabs are omnivorous, scavengers feeding on a variety of plants and animals, and are a chief predator of their own juveniles. Culture methods recommended zoeal stages be feed sea urchin embryos, Artemia nauplii, and/or rotifers (473). Zoea are both phytoplanktivorous and consume copepod nauplii. The megalopae stage is omnivorous and consumes fish larvae, small shell fish and aquatic plants. Juveniles and adults are described as general scavengers, bottom carnivores, detritivores and omnivores`, consuming whatever is in the area. Their main diet consists of molluscs (Rangia cuneata), crustaceans (xanthid crabs) and fish (704 710 355).

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial: Hard blue crabs were 197.8 million pounds for the United States commercial fishery, valued at $70.8 million. The Gulf region yielded 67.6 million pounds in landings (512). Soft shell crabs demand a higher price and are more abundant during the summer, at times of rapid growth. In Texas, minimum size is 5 inches carapace width, no females bearing eggs can be taken. No more than 300 marked crab traps can be used by any one person. The traps can be no larger than 18 cubic feet (721). In Mississippi, licenses are required to take crabs with more than six pots or traps, or trawl. Crabs are required to be greater than 5 inches in carapace width, and not in sponge between March 1 and June 30. Sponge crabs caught not during this period and north of the Inter coastal Waterway between Gulfport Ship Channel and the Mississippi-Alabama state line may be legally taken (478).

Recreational: The recreational catch can often exceed the commercial catch by up to four times (3). Similar regulations apply to recreational fishing with marked traps being labeled with name, address, saltwater stamp number, and date set out (722). In Mississippi crabs can be taken by hand line, drop net, dip net, hook and line and up to g crab pots/traps (478) .

Indicator: Several chlorinated hydrocarbons, cadmium and mercury were found to be acutely toxic to megalopal blue crabs in low concentrations (473). sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
April 19, 1990.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

Common Name: Blue crab
Scientific Name: Callinectes sapidus

FLELMR CODE: 5660

Other Common Names: Jimmies (males), sooks (adult females); common edible crab.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
	Family: Portunidae

Note: 	Subphylum: Crustacea

sections.heading: Range
sections.content:
Overall: Blue crab is a cosmopolitan species found in coastal waters, primarily in bays and brackish estuaries. The original range was from Nova Scotia and Maine to northern Argentina (767) .

Within the Study Area: It is abundant throughout the near shore and estuarine areas in
the Gulf of Mexico.

Migration and Movements
Migrations within estuarine systems are related to phases of life cycle, season, and to a lesser extent search for favorable environmental conditions. Most crabs move to relatively deeper, warmer waters during winter and return to rivers, tidal creeks, salt marshes and sounds when conditions become more favorable. Megalopae are recruited into estuarine waters followed by migration of early juvenile stages of both sexes upstream to lower salinity waters (686). In the Gulf of Mexico, immature females approaching their final molt during the spring, migrate to lower salinities to mate, then these females migrate back to higher salinity waters during June and July (3). Adult males appear to remain in lower salinity waters and rarely move to high salinity. Adult crabs rarely migrate between estuaries (3).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content: The eggs are carried by the female; when bearing the eggs the female is commonly referred to as a sponge crab. These females are found in 23-33 ppt and 19-29 C waters. Zoeae are planktonic and estuarine to oceanic. The megalopae swim freely and may be found in the surf area near the bottom in near shore or lower estuarine high-salinity areas. Juveniles and adults tend to be demersal and estuarine. Adult males spend most of their time in low salinity waters; females move into these lower salinities as they approach their terminal molt to mate. After mating, females move to higher salinity areas of estuaries and near shore environments for spawning.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.content:
Type: Depending on life stage, blue crabs are neritic, estuarine and riverine. Zoea are positively phototrophic (147).

Substrate: Juveniles and adults are found on muddy and sandy shores of the east and gulf coasts.

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Temperature: Tolerance limits for adults and juveniles range from 3-37 C, but are highly dependent on acclimation and salinity (705). The interaction of salinity and temperature reveals blue crabs to be less tolerant of low salinities at high temperatures and high salinities at low temperatures (455). The species has been found from 3-33 C. Adults cease feeding at temperatures around 10 C and burrow in mud at 5 C. Adult males are more tolerant of temperature extremes than females.

Salinity: Tolerant of extremes, the species has been found from freshwater to hypersaline lagoons (0-50 ppt). Early zoeae are found at high salinities, usually 20 ppt or greater (182). Megalopae may be transported to somewhat lower salinities. Juvenile, ?first crab?, gradually move into less saline waters (2-21 ppt most desirable). Reported values for juveniles vary and specific salinity levels are not critical to post larval crabs. Adult males are usually found at less than 10 ppt. Blue crabs are less tolerant of low salinities and high temperatures or of high salinities and low temperatures.

Dissolved Oxygen: Low dissolved oxygen concentrations coupled with high temperatures often results in high local mortalities throughout the summer season.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.content:
Repro Mode: Sexual, dioecious, internal fertilization.

Mating and Spawning: Mating normally occurs in low salinity waters in the upper reaches of tidal creeks and rivers at the females terminal molt. Females may ovulate more than once and sperm can survive for at least one year in the female`s seminal receptacle. Eggs are fertilized as they are passed from the ovaries to the seminal receptacle and are extruded out to the pleopods (473).

Season: In the Gulf of Mexico, two peak spawning periods typically occur, early spring and early fall (355 492).

Reproductive Capacity: 1.75 to 2 million eggs are produced per spawn.

sections.heading: Growth
sections.content:
Egg: When first extruded eggs are about 0.25 mrn. Hatching occurs at 14-17 days at 26 C and 12-14 days at 29 C; hatching does not appear to occur at salinities below 15 ppt (146 166).

Larva: Larvae 0.25 mm at hatching develop through 7 zoeal stages (approximately 31-49 days at 25 C and 26 ppt), the final zoeal stage is about 1.0 mrn in width. The last zoeal stage metamorphoses into a megalopa lasting 6-12 days, at optimum salinity (30 ppt) and temperature (25 C), before molting to the ?first crab? stage or juvenile at 2.2-3.0 mm (145).

Juvenile: Growth and maturation occur through a series of molts. Growth and molting stop during winter.

Adults: Blue crabs mature in approximately 10-12 months on the Gulf coast, while temperate populations may take up to 20 months (473). Females have varied in size from mature at 51 mm to immature at 177 mm. Females mate at their terminal molt, males continue to grow and molt after reaching sexual maturity. Blue crabs have an estimated life span of 3-4 years (704). Males are typically heavier than females of the same size. Growth equations for crabs > 25 mm CW are log W= -3.74 + 2.77 log (CW) male and log W= 3.54 + 2.64 log (CW) (575).

Food and Feeding
Blue crabs are omnivorous, scavengers feeding on a variety of plants and animals, and are a chief predator of their own juveniles. Culture methods recommended zoeal stages be feed sea urchin embryos, Artemia nauplii, and/or rotifers (473). Zoea are both phytoplanktivorous and consume copepod nauplii. The megalopae stage is omnivorous and consumes fish larvae, small shell fish and aquatic plants. Juveniles and adults are described as general scavengers, bottom carnivores, detritivores and omnivores`, consuming whatever is in the area. Their main diet consists of molluscs (Rangia cuneata), crustaceans (xanthid crabs) and fish (704 710 355).

sections.heading: Value
sections.content:
Commercial: Hard blue crabs were 197.8 million pounds for the United States commercial fishery, valued at $70.8 million. The Gulf region yielded 67.6 million pounds in landings (512). Soft shell crabs demand a higher price and are more abundant during the summer, at times of rapid growth. In Texas, minimum size is 5 inches carapace width, no females bearing eggs can be taken. No more than 300 marked crab traps can be used by any one person. The traps can be no larger than 18 cubic feet (721). In Mississippi, licenses are required to take crabs with more than six pots or traps, or trawl. Crabs are required to be greater than 5 inches in carapace width, and not in sponge between March 1 and June 30. Sponge crabs caught not during this period and north of the Inter coastal Waterway between Gulfport Ship Channel and the Mississippi-Alabama state line may be legally taken (478).

Recreational: The recreational catch can often exceed the commercial catch by up to four times (3). Similar regulations apply to recreational fishing with marked traps being labeled with name, address, saltwater stamp number, and date set out (722). In Mississippi crabs can be taken by hand line, drop net, dip net, hook and line and up to g crab pots/traps (478) .
